title: Wealth doesn't help
hookLine: an estate sale lays a life out on folding tables; the Buddha says carry it out of the burning house first (AN 3.52)
tomorrow: if even the body stays behind, what goes on?

lines: SO WHAT DO YOU DO WITH IT NOW?
cards: Estate sales have their own hush. A whole life laid out on folding tables: the good dishes, a coat with the tags still on, a drawer of chargers, all with little price stickers. Everything the person kept is still here.
They aren't. You can't take it with you. Everyone knows the line.
So what do you do with it now? The Buddha's answer came to two old men who asked him almost exactly that.

teach.b: In the Anguttara Nikaya, two brahmins, old and frail, come to the Buddha. They say they haven't done good things or built any shelter against what's coming, and they ask him to teach them. He answers with a fire.
The world is burning, he says, with aging, sickness and death.
When a house is on fire, the pot you carry out is the one that's useful to you, not the one that burns inside. So, since the world is burning, carry things out by giving.
What's given is well carried out. That flips the estate sale. The stickers mark what stayed behind.
The things that went on were given away before. The Dhammapada adds the inside view.
My children, my wealth, a foolish person thinks, and is tormented; but he isn't even his own, so how can children and wealth be? None of this calls money bad.
Earlier in the path, the suttas praised earning honestly and saving wisely. It only says what wealth can't do: come along.
It stays behind. What goes on is what you did with it, while the house was still standing.

how: Giving (dana) is a central lay Buddhist practice: people give food to monks, support temples and charities, and some families make offerings in the name of a relative who has died.

o: being rich gets in the way of meditation
possessions can't come with you when you die
wealth can't buy friends who really care

games.q: the burning house — tap the pairs.
p: no shelter built against what's coming

s: the Buddha taught that money itself is bad
the suttas praise earning honestly and saving wisely; the point is that wealth can't come along.
in the sutta, what's given is what's 'carried out' of the burning house
the pot carried out is useful; the one left inside burns.
it's too late for the two old men to do any good
they ask, and the Buddha answers: carry things out by giving, starting now.

games.q: your great-aunt is leaving everything to relatives 'after i'm gone' and gives nothing now. she asks what the burning-house sutta would say.
o: nothing; what happens after death is all that matters for giving.
give some now, while the house stands: what's given is carried out.
give everything away today and keep nothing for herself.
games.why: the Buddha tells the old men to carry things out by giving, while there's still time. it's not all-or-nothing; it's now rather than later.

practice: Choose one thing you own that someone else would use more than you do: a book, a jacket, a spare charger. Hold it, or picture it, and set it apart right now, by the door or in a bag.
Then sit with the small lightness of something already on its way out of the house.

wordCard.voice: Wealth doesn't help: at death, everything owned stays behind. What's given goes on.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity; how the burning-house sutta says to carry things out.

carryVoice: The day's line: it stays behind, and what's given is carried out. Day sixteen thirty-six, lighter.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.52 (two old brahmins; the world burning with aging, sickness and death; what is given is well taken out of the burning house)
Dhammapada 62 ('my sons, my wealth': the fool is tormented; he is not even his own)
